title: The past tense: weak verbs
goal: Tell what has already happened using the biggest verb group — the one that adds an ending without changing anything inside the word.
bekal: form the past tense of -a group and -i group verbs
describe your weekend in a few sentences

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Um helgina
dialogs.intro: Monday morning at school. Búdí has just come back from his first trip outside Reykjavík.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: What did you do over the weekend?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég ferðaðist til Þingvalla með Siggu.
lines.id: I took a trip to Þingvellir with Sigga.
lines.literal: I traveled to Þingvellir with Sigga.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Frábært! Við keyrðum í tvo tíma og gengum lengi.
lines.id: Great! We drove for two hours and walked for a long time.
lines.literal: great! we drove in two hours and walked long.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já. Sigga sagði mér að höfðingjar hittust þar til forna.
lines.id: Yes. Sigga told me the chieftains used to meet there.
lines.literal: yes. Sigga told me that chieftains met there of old.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Rétt. Alþingi var stofnað þar árið 930.
lines.id: That's right. The Alþingi was founded there in 930.
lines.literal: right. Alþingi was founded there year-the 930.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég trúði því varla. Elsta þing í heimi!
lines.id: I could hardly believe it. The oldest parliament in the world!
lines.literal: I believed it hardly. oldest parliament in world!

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Og gjáin? Fannst þér hún merkileg?
lines.id: And the gorge? Did you find it interesting?
lines.literal: and gorge-the? seemed to-you it interesting?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já — ég stóð á milli tveggja heimsálfa!
lines.id: Yes — I stood between two continents!
lines.literal: yes — I stood in between two continents.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Nákvæmlega. Ameríka öðrum megin, Evrópa hinum.
lines.id: Exactly. America on one side, Europe on the other.
lines.literal: exactly. America one side, Europe the-other.

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Ég gleymi þessu aldrei. Takk fyrir ábendinguna!
lines.id: I'll never forget it. Thanks for the tip!
lines.literal: I forget this never. thanks for tip-the!

notes: **Weak verbs add an ending without changing the inside of the word.** *Tala → talaði*, *keyra → keyrði*, *trúa → trúði*. This is the biggest group, so once you've mastered it, you can already put together most stories about the past.

**There are only two kinds of ending**: **-aði** for -a group verbs (*tala*, *skoða*, *borða*), and **-di / -ti / -ddi** for the -i group (*keyra*, *læra*, *trúa*). The choice among those three depends on the sound before it, not on memorization.
**The *ég* and *hann* forms are always the same** in the past — just as in the present. Only *þú* (add *-r*) and the plural forms differ.

**A few words in this dialog are strong, not weak**: *var*, *gengum*, *stóð*, *fannst*. Their vowel changes instead of an ending being added. That group is unit 16 — for now, just notice that they exist.
**Um helgina takes þolfall** because it names a **length of time**: *um helgina* (over the weekend), *í tvo tíma* (for two hours). For a point in time the case is different: *á morgun*, *um kvöldið*.

**Þingvellir is more than a tourist spot.** In that valley, in 930, the free men of Iceland founded the *Alþingi* — a parliament still running today and therefore called the oldest in the world. In the same place, in 1944, Iceland proclaimed its independence from Denmark.

grammars.title: The two groups of weak verbs
body: Six forms each, and the ending pattern repeats exactly. Notice *u-hljóðvarp* showing up again in the plural of the first group: *tala → töluðum*.
after: The **-aði** group is the friendliest and most productive: almost every new verb that enters Icelandic joins it. If you're not sure, *-aði* is your best guess.
The past tense never uses a helper like "did" or "have". *Ég talaði* already means "I spoke" — just like the English simple past.

grammars.title: Choosing -di, -ti, or -ddi
body: It's not memorization, it's sound. Listen to the last letter before the ending.

head: Letter before
Ending
Example
Þátíð
rows: voiced: l, m, n, r, f, g, ð

after: The reason makes sense in terms of sound: after a letter where your throat vibrates, the ending vibrates too (**-ði**); after one where it doesn't, the ending doesn't either (**-ti**). You can feel it yourself by touching your throat as you say them — just like the *d* in English *played* versus the *t* sound in *walked*.
⚠️ *Kaupa → keypti* also changes its vowel. A few weak verbs do this: *segja → sagði*, *þykja → þótti*, *sækja → sótti*. There aren't many, but they're all common.

blocks.text: These fifteen verbs cover most everyday stories. Say each row as a pair — *tala, talaði* — until the switch feels automatic; that's far quicker than memorizing tables of forms.

sections.title: Þingvellir: the valley where a nation was born

blocks.text: Forty minutes from Reykjavík, a valley is split by a long gorge called *Almannagjá*. The gorge wasn't carved by a river; it's a **rift between two continental plates** that drift two centimeters apart every year. Standing inside it means standing between America and Europe.

blocks.title: Three dates in one valley
items: **930** — the free men gathered for the first time and founded the Alþingi. Laws were memorized, not written down, and recited aloud from *Lögberg* every summer.
**1000** — in the same place, Iceland decided to adopt Christianity through negotiation, not war.
**1944** — the Icelandic republic was proclaimed in that valley, before tens of thousands of people who had walked there in the rain.

exercises.prompt: Change into the past tense (*ég* form).
Fill in the blanks with the right past tense form.

items: What did you do over the weekend?
I took a trip to Þingvellir.
